blocks.title: About this page
blocks.text: Written for this site as of November 2026 for a fresher who wants experienced-level depth, in the style of the Java Full Stack guides. Every example titled `*.py` was run when this page was built, on Python 3.12.13 with FastAPI 0.162.0, Pydantic 2.14.2, SQLAlchemy 2.1.8, Django 6.1.3, and the output shown is what it really printed. Python and its libraries change quickly (and some examples need servers that a build cannot start, so those are only syntax-checked): check the official documentation for anything newer before relying on a detail.

Part 7 introduced decorators as "function in, wrapper out". The full picture has four variants, and every serious framework uses all of them (`@app.get`, `@pytest.fixture`, `@dataclass`, `@property`, `@login_required`).

blocks.title: Decorators.py

blocks.text:
Rules for decorators you will be asked to write:

1. **Always `functools.wraps`**: it preserves `__name__`, `__doc__`, `__wrapped__` and the signature, which FastAPI, pytest, Sphinx and debuggers read. Class-based decorators use `functools.update_wrapper`.
2. **Forward `*args, **kwargs`** and the return value.
3. **Decorating methods works naturally** because `self` is just the first argument; a *class-based* decorator on a method needs a `__get__` (descriptors, next chapter) to bind it.
4. **Async functions** need an `async def wrapper` that `await`s the wrapped call; a sync wrapper around a coroutine function would return an un-awaited coroutine.
5. **Order matters** when stacking: the decorator nearest the function is applied first (`@tag("i")` wraps `text`, then `@tag("b")` wraps that), as the output shows.

Check `inspect.iscoroutinefunction(func)` and return an `async def wrapper` that records `time.perf_counter()` around `await func(...)`; otherwise a sync wrapper. Mention `functools.wraps`, use `try/finally` so the time is recorded on exceptions too, and that for production you would emit a metric (Prometheus histogram) rather than print.
blocks.title: Write a decorator that times a function, then make it work with async functions

blocks.text: A **descriptor** is an object with `__get__`, and optionally `__set__` and `__delete__`, stored as a **class attribute**. When an attribute is looked up on an instance, Python checks the class for a descriptor first and calls its methods. This one mechanism implements `property`, methods, `classmethod`, `staticmethod`, `__slots__` and the fields of Django and SQLAlchemy models.

blocks.title: Descriptors.py
Output

blocks.text:
| Kind | Defines | Lookup precedence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Data descriptor** | `__get__` and `__set__` (or `__delete__`) | Beats the instance `__dict__` |
| **Non-data descriptor** | only `__get__` (functions, `classmethod`, `cached_property`) | The instance `__dict__` wins over it |
| Plain class attribute | no descriptor methods | Instance `__dict__` wins |

### `__getattr__`, `__getattribute__` and `__setattr__`

blocks.code:
class Config:
    def __init__(self, **values):
        self.__dict__["_values"] = dict(values)

    def __getattr__(self, name):                   # called ONLY when normal lookup fails
        try:
            return self._values[name]
        except KeyError:
            raise AttributeError(f"no setting {name!r}") from None

    def __setattr__(self, name, value):            # called for EVERY assignment
        print(f"set {name}")
        self._values[name] = value


c = Config(host="localhost")
print(c.host)
c.port = 8000
print(c.port, hasattr(c, "missing"))
blocks.title: Hooks.py

blocks.text: `__getattr__` is a **fallback** for missing attributes (proxies, lazy loading, dynamic APIs); `__getattribute__` runs for **every** access and is easy to make infinitely recursive, so use it only when you must. Reading `self.x` inside them needs care: go through `object.__getattribute__` or `self.__dict__`.

Django model fields (`name = models.CharField()`), SQLAlchemy columns (`Mapped[str]`), Pydantic and dataclass fields, `@property`, `@cached_property`, `functools.partialmethod` and every bound method are all descriptors. When a framework "magically" turns a class attribute into per-instance data and per-class metadata, a descriptor (often with `__set_name__`) is how.
blocks.title: Where descriptors hide

blocks.text: A class is an instance of its **metaclass**; by default `type`. The `class` statement is a convenient way to call `type(name, bases, namespace)`, which you can also do by hand to create classes at run time:

blocks.title: Metaclass.py

blocks.code:
hello generated type Dynamic
['csv', 'jsonexporter'] True
TypeError: Sloppy.missing needs a docstring
RequireDocstrings True
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text:
| Tool | When |
| --- | --- |
| **Class decorator** | Modify or register a class after it is built. Simplest |
| **`__init_subclass__`** | React to subclassing: plugin registries, validation, default attributes. Covers most "metaclass" needs |
| **`__set_name__`** | A descriptor learns its attribute name |
| **Metaclass** | Change class *creation* itself: control the namespace (`__prepare__`), inject methods, build a model from field declarations (Django ORM, SQLAlchemy declarative, `Enum`, `ABCMeta`) |

"Metaclasses are deeper magic than 99% of users should ever worry about" (Tim Peters). They complicate inheritance (conflicting metaclasses), debugging and tool support. Reach for a decorator, `__init_subclass__` or composition first. You need to *understand* them because frameworks use them, not because your code should.
blocks.title: Metaclasses are a last resort

blocks.text: Python lets a program inspect itself, which is the basis of dependency injection, serialisation, ORMs, test discovery and API frameworks.

blocks.code:
import inspect
from dataclasses import dataclass, fields
from typing import Annotated, get_type_hints


def create_user(name: str, age: int = 18, *tags: str, active: bool = True) -> dict:
    """Create a user."""


sig = inspect.signature(create_user)
for param in sig.parameters.values():
    default = "required" if param.default is inspect.Parameter.empty else param.default
    print(f"{param.name:<8} {param.kind.name:<17} annotation={getattr(param.annotation, '__name__', param.annotation)} default={default}")
print(sig.return_annotation.__name__, get_type_hints(create_user)["age"])


@dataclass
class Item:
    name: str
    price: float = 0.0

    def total(self, qty: int) -> float:
        return self.price * qty

print([f.name for f in fields(Item)], [n for n, _ in inspect.getmembers(Item, inspect.isfunction)][:3])
item = Item("pen", 2.5)
method = getattr(item, "total")                       # attribute access by NAME at run time
print(method(4), hasattr(item, "colour"), getattr(item, "colour", "none"))
setattr(item, "colour", "blue")
print(vars(item), type(item).__mro__[0].__name__, callable(method), inspect.isclass(Item))

# How a framework decides what to inject: it reads the signature of YOUR function
def handler(request, user_id: int, db):
    pass

print([p for p in inspect.signature(handler).parameters])

blocks.text:
The last lines are the idea behind **FastAPI**: it calls `inspect.signature` on your endpoint, reads each parameter's name, annotation and default, and decides whether it comes from the path, the query string, the body or a dependency. That is why `functools.wraps` matters in decorators (it keeps the signature visible), and why type hints are a runtime API as well as documentation.

| Function | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `type(x)`, `isinstance`, `issubclass` | Type tests |
| `dir(x)`, `vars(x)`, `x.__dict__` | Names available; instance attributes |
| `getattr`, `setattr`, `hasattr`, `delattr` | Attribute access by string |
| `inspect.signature`, `getmembers`, `getsource`, `iscoroutinefunction` | Structure of callables and modules |
| `typing.get_type_hints(obj)` | Resolved annotations (including forward references) |
| `importlib.metadata.entry_points()` | Plugins registered by installed packages |

`import shop.orders` does four things: look the name up in `sys.modules` (a cache), and if absent **find** the module (finders walk `sys.path`), **load** it (compile or read `.pyc`, execute the top-level code **once**) and **bind** the result. Because the module object is cached, a module is effectively a **singleton**, and top-level code is the right place for definitions but the wrong place for side effects.

blocks.code:
import importlib
import pathlib
import sys

root = pathlib.Path("demo")
(root / "shop").mkdir(parents=True)
(root / "shop" / "__init__.py").write_text("print('shop package imported')\nVERSION = '1.0'\n")
(root / "shop" / "orders.py").write_text("print('orders module executed')\ndef count():\n    return 3\n")
(root / "shop" / "util.py").write_text("from . import orders          # relative import\ndef twice():\n    return orders.count() * 2\n")
sys.path.insert(0, str(root))

import shop.orders                                  # runs shop/__init__.py, then orders.py
import shop.orders as again                         # second import: served from sys.modules, nothing printed
print(shop.orders is again, "shop.orders" in sys.modules, shop.VERSION)

from shop.util import twice
print(twice())

module = importlib.import_module("shop." + "orders")   # import by name computed at run time
print(module.__name__, module.__file__.endswith("orders.py"), module.__package__)

(root / "shop" / "orders.py").write_text("print('orders v2')\ndef count():\n    return 30\n")
importlib.invalidate_caches()
print(shop.orders.count())                          # unchanged: the module object is cached
importlib.reload(shop.orders)                       # explicit re-execution (rarely a good idea)
print(shop.orders.count())

namespace = root / "ns_pkg"                         # a folder WITHOUT __init__.py is a namespace package
namespace.mkdir()
(namespace / "a.py").write_text("X = 1\n")
import ns_pkg.a
print(ns_pkg.a.X, ns_pkg.__file__)

blocks.text:
### Circular imports

Two modules that import each other at the top level can fail, because the first is only **partially initialised** when the second asks for it:

blocks.code:
import pathlib
import sys

pathlib.Path("a.py").write_text("from b import b_func\n\ndef a_func():\n    return 'a'\n")
pathlib.Path("b.py").write_text("from a import a_func\n\ndef b_func():\n    return 'b'\n")
sys.path.insert(0, ".")

try:
    import a
except ImportError as error:
    print("ImportError:", str(error).split(" (")[0])

# Fix 1: import the MODULE and use the attribute later; Fix 2: import inside the function; Fix 3: move shared code to a third module
pathlib.Path("c.py").write_text("import d\n\ndef c_func():\n    return 'c' + d.d_func()\n")
pathlib.Path("d.py").write_text("def d_func():\n    import c                      # deferred import: runs only when called\n    return 'd'\n")
import c
print(c.c_func())
blocks.title: Circular.py

blocks.code:
ImportError: cannot import name 'a_func' from partially initialized module 'a'
cd
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text: Import rules for large codebases: use **absolute imports** at module top; **relative imports** only inside a package; no `from x import *` (it hides where names come from and defeats linters); put an `__all__` list in a package's public module to define its API; keep top-level code free of I/O, and move heavy imports (pandas, torch) inside the functions that need them when start-up time matters (`python -X importtime -c "import app"` shows the cost of each import). Python 3.15 is expected to add an explicit *lazy import* syntax (PEP 810); until then, deferred imports inside functions are the tool.

- `sys.modules` caches modules: top-level code runs once; a module is a singleton.
- `sys.path` is searched in order: script folder, `PYTHONPATH`, standard library, `site-packages`.
- Package = folder with `__init__.py` (or a namespace package without it). Absolute imports by default; `from . import x` inside a package.
- Circular imports: import the module not the name, defer the import into the function, or extract shared code.
- Never name a file after a library (`random.py`, `email.py`); never `import *`.
- `importlib.import_module(name)` for dynamic imports; `importlib.metadata.entry_points` for plugins; `-X importtime` for start-up cost.

sections.title: Calling Native Code: ctypes, struct and C Extensions

blocks.text:
Python often wraps C: NumPy, `cryptography`, `lxml`, `psycopg`, `orjson`, `uvloop`, PyTorch. You meet native code in three ways:

| Approach | What it is | When |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **`ctypes`** (standard library) | Call functions in shared libraries directly from Python, describe C structs | Quick bindings to an existing library, no compiler |
| **`cffi`** | Cleaner foreign-function interface from C declarations | Larger bindings, PyPy-friendly |
| **C extension / Cython / pybind11 / PyO3 (Rust)** | Compiled modules using the CPython C API | Performance-critical code, new native libraries |

blocks.code:
import ctypes
import struct

class Point(ctypes.Structure):                       # a C struct in memory
    _fields_ = [("x", ctypes.c_int32), ("y", ctypes.c_int32)]

p = Point(3, 4)
print(ctypes.sizeof(p), p.x + p.y, bytes(p).hex())

buffer = ctypes.create_string_buffer(b"hello", 16)    # a mutable C char[16]
print(len(buffer), buffer.value, buffer.raw[:6])

packed = struct.pack("<I H 4s", 258, 7, b"abcd")      # fixed binary layouts: network and file formats
print(packed.hex(), struct.unpack("<I H 4s", packed), struct.calcsize("<IH4s"))

view = memoryview(bytearray(b"abcdef"))               # zero-copy slices of a buffer
part = view[2:5]
part[0] = ord("X")
print(bytes(view))
blocks.title: Native.py

blocks.text: `struct` packs and unpacks fixed binary layouts (network protocols, file headers); `memoryview` exposes the **buffer protocol** so that slicing does not copy; `ctypes` maps C types. Calling a real library function is `ctypes.CDLL("libname").function`, with `argtypes` and `restype` set explicitly, because a wrong signature crashes the interpreter instead of raising an exception.

A bad pointer in `ctypes`, or a bug in a C extension, produces a segmentation fault that no `try/except` can catch, taking down the worker. Enable `faulthandler` (below) in production so a crash leaves a Python traceback, pin extension versions, and isolate risky native work in a subprocess.
blocks.title: Native code can crash the whole process

blocks.text:
Most production problems fall into a few shapes. Match the symptom to the tool:

| Symptom | First look | Tools |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Exception in logs | The last traceback line, then the frame in your code | `logger.exception`, Sentry, `traceback` |
| Wrong result | Reproduce minimally; print intermediate values | `breakpoint()`, `pdb`, tests, `repr()` |
| Hangs / stuck request | Where is every thread right now? | `py-spy dump --pid`, `faulthandler.dump_traceback_later(30)` |
| High CPU | Which function? | `py-spy top`, `cProfile`, `pyinstrument` |
| Memory growing | Who allocates, who holds | `tracemalloc`, `memray`, `objgraph` |
| Slow start-up | Which imports? | `python -X importtime` |
| Crash with no traceback | A native fault | `faulthandler` / `python -X faulthandler`, core dump |
| Works locally, fails in the container | Different Python, packages or encoding | `python -VV`, `pip freeze`, `sys.path`, `locale`, `PYTHONUTF8` |
| Warnings you ignore | They become errors in the next release | `python -W error`, `-X dev` |

blocks.code:
import faulthandler
import sys


def inner():
    faulthandler.dump_traceback(file=sys.stdout, all_threads=False)   # what every thread is doing, right now


def outer():
    inner()


outer()
blocks.title: Faulthandler.py

blocks.code:
Stack (most recent call first):
  File "main.py", line 6 in inner
  File "main.py", line 10 in outer
  File "main.py", line 13 in <module>
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text:
`faulthandler.dump_traceback_later(30, repeat=True)` prints every thread's stack if the program is still running after 30 seconds, which is the cheapest way to see **why a process is hung**; `python -X faulthandler` or `faulthandler.enable()` also dumps the traceback on a crash. Add `-X dev` (or `PYTHONDEVMODE=1`) in tests to enable extra runtime checks, such as resource warnings for unclosed files and the asyncio debug mode.

### A short debugging method

1. **Read the whole traceback** from the bottom; identify the first frame in *your* code.
2. **Reproduce** with the smallest input; write it as a failing test.
3. **Form one hypothesis** and test it (a print, a `breakpoint()`, an assertion), instead of changing things at random.
4. **Check assumptions about the environment**: which interpreter, which versions, which environment variables.
5. **Fix the cause**, keep the test, and add logging or a metric if the failure was hard to see.

Get a stack dump of the live process without restarting it (`py-spy dump --pid <pid>` or a `faulthandler` timer or signal handler), look for threads blocked on locks, sockets or queues, and for an event loop stuck in a blocking call. Check external dependencies (database locks, a call without a timeout), then thread and connection pool saturation. Fix with timeouts, bounded pools and, for asyncio, removing blocking calls. Then add the signal that would have caught it: a latency alert, a health check that exercises the dependency.
blocks.title: "A Python service hangs in production. What do you do?"

blocks.text: #### Decorators in Depth

items.question: What does `@decorator` do exactly?
items.answer: It is syntax for `func = decorator(func)` executed once, when the function is defined. For `@decorator(args)` Python first calls `decorator(args)` and applies the returned callable to the function. Class decorators work the same way on a class.

items.question: Why does a decorated function show the wrong name without `functools.wraps`?
items.answer: The returned wrapper is a different function named `wrapper`, so `__name__`, `__doc__` and the signature belong to it. `wraps` copies the original metadata onto the wrapper (and sets `__wrapped__`), so tools see what you expect.

items.question: How would you apply the same behaviour to every method of a class?
items.answer: Use a class decorator that loops over the class namespace and wraps each callable (`for name, value in vars(cls).items(): ...setattr(cls, name, deco(value))`), or implement `__init_subclass__` or a metaclass. Think twice: explicit decoration is usually clearer.

blocks.text: #### Descriptors and the Attribute Machinery

items.question: What is a descriptor and where is it stored?
items.answer: An object implementing `__get__` (and optionally `__set__`/`__delete__`) that is stored as an attribute of a **class**. Attribute access on instances is routed through it, which is how properties, methods, `classmethod` and ORM fields are implemented.

items.question: What is the difference between a data and a non-data descriptor?
items.answer: A data descriptor defines `__set__` or `__delete__` as well as `__get__` and takes precedence over the instance dictionary; a non-data descriptor only defines `__get__`, so an instance attribute of the same name overrides it. Functions are non-data descriptors, which is why you can shadow a method on one instance.

items.question: When is `__getattr__` called, compared with `__getattribute__`?
items.answer: `__getattribute__` is called for every attribute access; `__getattr__` is called only after normal lookup (instance, class, bases) has raised `AttributeError`. Implement `__getattr__` for fallbacks; override `__getattribute__` rarely and carefully.

blocks.text: #### Classes Are Objects: `type`, `__init_subclass__` and Metaclasses

items.question: What is a metaclass?
items.answer: The class of a class: the callable that builds a class object from its name, bases and namespace. By default it is `type`. A custom metaclass can validate or transform the class body, register classes or add methods; `ABCMeta` and `EnumMeta` are examples in the standard library.

items.question: How can you create a class dynamically?
items.answer: Call `type(name, bases, namespace)` (or `types.new_class` for more control). It returns a class object just like the `class` statement would.

items.question: When would you choose `__init_subclass__` over a metaclass?
items.answer: Whenever you only need to run code when a subclass is defined (register it, validate attributes, set defaults). It is simpler, composes with multiple inheritance and does not create metaclass conflicts.

blocks.text: #### Introspection and Reflection

items.question: How does FastAPI know which arguments of your function come from the request?
items.answer: It inspects the function's signature (`inspect.signature` and type hints): parameters that match path placeholders come from the path, parameters with simple types from the query string, Pydantic model types from the body, and parameters whose default is `Depends(...)` from a dependency. The annotations are read at run time.

items.question: When is `getattr(obj, name)` better than `obj.name`?
items.answer: When the attribute name is data (from configuration, a request or a loop): dispatching to `handle_<command>` methods, serialising fields by name, plugin lookup. Never pass untrusted names to `getattr`/`setattr`, since they can reach internal attributes.

blocks.text: #### Modules and the Import System

items.question: What happens when you import a module twice?
items.answer: The first import finds, compiles and executes it, then stores the module object in `sys.modules`. The second import returns that cached object, so the top-level code does not run again. `importlib.reload` re-executes it explicitly.

items.question: Why do circular imports fail and how do you fix them?
items.answer: When `a` imports `b` during its own initialisation and `b` imports names from `a`, the module `a` exists in `sys.modules` but has not defined those names yet. Fix by restructuring (move shared code into a third module), importing the module instead of the name, or importing inside the function that needs it.

items.question: What is the difference between a regular package and a namespace package?
items.answer: A regular package has an `__init__.py` and lives in one directory. A namespace package has no `__init__.py` and can be spread over several directories on `sys.path`, which lets separately installed distributions contribute to one package name.

blocks.text: #### Calling Native Code: ctypes, struct and C Extensions

items.question: When would you write a C extension or use Cython instead of staying in Python?
items.answer: When profiling shows a small hot loop dominating run time that cannot be vectorised with NumPy or sped up algorithmically, or when you need to wrap an existing C/C++/Rust library. Cython, pybind11 and PyO3 make this far less painful than hand-written C API code.

items.question: What is the buffer protocol and why does it matter?
items.answer: A C-level interface that lets objects (`bytes`, `bytearray`, `array`, NumPy arrays, `mmap`) expose their raw memory so that others can read or write it without copying. `memoryview` is the Python face, and it is how large binary data is handled efficiently.

blocks.text: #### Troubleshooting Playbook and Diagnostics Toolbox

items.question: How do you find out why a Python process is stuck?
items.answer: Dump the stacks of all threads: `py-spy dump --pid`, `faulthandler.dump_traceback_later` or a signal-triggered dump. Look at what each thread (or the single event-loop thread) is waiting on: a lock, a socket read without timeout, a queue, a blocking call inside a coroutine.

items.question: What does `python -X dev` give you?
items.answer: Development mode enables additional runtime checks: warnings for resource leaks (unclosed files), asyncio debug mode, faulthandler, stricter memory-allocator checks and more visible deprecation warnings. Use it in tests and CI to catch problems early.
